title: The effect of limited English proficiency and interpreter service use on clinical outcomes in psychiatric inpatient units
author: Daly

evds.title: LEP psychiatric inpatients received more consultant reviews (median 4 vs 3) but not after adjusting for length of stay
evds.finding: LEP psychiatric inpatients were reviewed by consultants more often than EP patients (median 4 vs 3 reviews, p=0.036) (Table 1). The difference disappeared once the number of consultant reviews was normalized by length of stay, suggesting the extra reviews tracked longer admissions rather than a per-day increase in consultant effort.

evds.title: Median psychiatric inpatient length of stay was higher for LEP patients (12 vs 8 days) but not statistically significant
evds.finding: Across three adult psychiatric inpatient units, the median length of stay was higher for patients with limited English proficiency (LEP) than for English-proficient (EP) patients — 12 vs 8 days — but the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.155) (Table 1).

evds.title: No LEP psychiatric inpatients received a personality disorder diagnosis versus 19% of English-proficient patients
evds.finding: Discharge diagnoses differed significantly between groups (p=0.018): none of the 47 LEP patients received a primary discharge diagnosis of personality disorder, versus 9 of 47 (19%) English-proficient patients, with adjusted standardised residuals (±3.2) flagging the personality-disorder cell as the driver (Table 1). The authors raise a language barrier during assessment as one candidate explanation for the absent diagnoses.

candidates: The length of stay difference between patients with limited English proficiency (LEP) and proficient English patients was not statistically significant (p=0.155).
Patients with limited English proficiency underwent more consultant reviews compared to English proficient patients (p=0.036).
Patients with limited English proficiency had different discharge diagnoses, with no primary discharge diagnoses of personality disorder being made for this group (p=0.018).

abstractAnchors.text: An increased length of stay for those with LEP was not statistically significant (p=0.155).
The LEP group did undergo more consultant reviews (p=0.036), however, and attracted different discharge diagnoses, with no primary discharge diagnoses of personality disorder made (p=0.018).
This study provides evidence of significant effects of limited English on both service burden and outcome.
